questions.q: A team ships a checkout redesign because a test was significant, but the redesign actually does nothing. Which error is this?
options: Type II error
Type I error
Not an error, because the result was significant
A power calculation error
questions.explain: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error (a false alarm), which occurs with probability alpha.

questions.q: A test has 80% power. What does that mean?
options: There is an 80% chance the null hypothesis is true
The p-value will be 0.20
If the effect of the assumed size is real, the test will detect it about 80% of the time
The test has an 80% false-alarm rate
questions.explain: Power = 1 - beta, the probability of rejecting the null when a real effect of the assumed size exists.

questions.q: In the simulation, 30 customers per group detected a real $7.50 lift only about 48% of the time. What is the best interpretation of a non-significant result from such a test?
options: Inconclusive: the test was underpowered, so it can't rule out a real effect
Proof that the lift is zero
Proof that the null is true
Evidence that alpha was set too high
questions.explain: With low power, non-significance is common even when an effect exists, so it cannot be read as 'no effect'.

questions.q: Which change increases power, holding everything else fixed?
options: Reducing the sample size
Choosing a smaller effect to look for
Increasing the sample size
Increasing the noise in the metric
questions.explain: More data shrinks the standard error, making a real effect easier to distinguish from noise.

questions.q: Why does detecting a small effect (d = 0.2) require far more data than a large one (d = 0.8)?
options: Small effects are always false
Statistical tests only work on large effects
Alpha must be smaller for small effects
A small effect is closer to the noise, so the standard error must shrink much further to separate them
questions.explain: Required n scales with 1/d squared. Going from d = 0.8 to 0.2 multiplies the needed sample by 16.
